# Lynn Conway
Lynn Conway (1938–2024) was a pioneering computer scientist and electrical engineer whose career significantly impacted microelectronics and VLSI (very-large-scale integration) chip design. After beginning at IBM in the 1960s, where she invented multiple-issue out-of-order dynamic instruction scheduling for supercomputers, Conway faced discrimination when attempting a gender transition and was fired by IBM in 1968, a decision for which the company formally apologized over fifty years later. Undeterred, she resumed her career post-transition, working at Memorex before joining Xerox PARC, where she led the development of dimensionless, scalable design rules and the multiproject wafers (MPW) technology. Conway co-authored the influential textbook *Introduction to VLSI Systems* (with Carver Mead), laying the foundation for modern chip design methodology and fostering the rise of the electronic design automation and foundry models.
Conway served as a visiting professor at MIT and later as associate dean and professor at the University of Michigan, focusing on visual communications and user interface control systems, before retiring as emerita in 1998. Beyond her technical achievements, Conway was a leading advocate for transgender rights, sharing her personal story and supporting others in transition, while campaigning for equitable treatment in technology and academia. She identified and named the "Conway effect," describing the phenomenon of overlooked innovators from marginalized groups. Widely recognized, she received numerous awards, including the IEEE Computer Pioneer Award, membership in the National Academy of Engineering, and induction into the National Inventors Hall of Fame. Conway passed away in June 2024 at age 86, leaving a legacy in both engineering innovation and social activism.
